opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what struck me most in that first conversation was how little time we spent talking about any single trick or model architecture. I went in half-expecting a pitch: here's our secret sauce, here's the benchmark we beat. Instead it felt much more like a research group thinking out loud about first principles.

The question they kept coming back to was: what would it actually take to build a general-purpose brain for robots, rather than a system that's very good at one task in one lab? That framing changes a lot. You stop asking "how do I get this grasp to 95 percent success" and start asking "what kind of data, at what scale and diversity, would let a model pick up skills the way language models picked up language?"

The other thing I noticed was the comfort with uncertainty. Nobody claimed to have the answer. People were very candid about what wasn't working, where data was messy, where a model generalized in surprising ways and where it fell flat. For me that was a strong signal. In robotics it's easy to be seduced by a nice demo video, and I appreciated a culture that cared more about understanding why something worked than about how it looked.

And finally, there was this sense that the hardware, the data collection, and the learning side weren't separate silos. Researchers cared about how teleoperation was done and how tasks were chosen, because they saw that as part of the research itself. That integrated view, treating the whole loop as the problem, is what shaped my impression most. It felt less like a typical company and more like a group making a long-term bet on a particular way of doing science.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, that first conversation actually caught me a little off guard, because I came in expecting to talk about robots, and we barely talked about hardware at all. What they wanted to talk about was data. Where it comes from, how much of it you need, what it means for a model to generalize across embodiments. It was clear very quickly that they weren't thinking of this as a robotics company in the traditional sense. They were thinking of it as a foundation model problem that happens to have a body attached.

The thing that stuck with me most was how honest they were about what they didn't know. There was no pitch deck energy. Someone would say something confident, and then two minutes later someone else would push back and say, well, we actually haven't shown that yet. And nobody got defensive. That kind of culture is rarer than people think, especially in a field where everyone is under pressure to produce a demo video.

The other impression was patience. A lot of robotics efforts get pulled toward a specific task, a specific customer, a specific form factor, because that's where the near-term revenue is. The team was very deliberate about resisting that. They talked about laundry folding and clearing tables not because those are products, but because they're hard, messy, long-horizon problems that expose the weaknesses of a model. It was research chosen as a stress test, not as a use case.

So I walked out thinking, these are people who have taken the lessons from language models seriously and are willing to sit in a long, uncomfortable middle period while the data and the methods catch up. That shaped how I understood everything they did afterward.

But the question they were interested in was broader: how do you build intelligence that can transfer across tasks and different physical situations? That made the conversation feel very open. There was a big ambition, but also a willingness to talk about what we don’t yet understand and what experiments might help us figure it out.
